title: Install Git Bash on Windows
summary: Windows-only setup of Git for Windows so VS Code can use Git Bash as its terminal. Mac users skip it because Bash is already available.

concepts.heading: Installing Git for Windows
points: Download the installer from gitforwindows.org (Git SCM) and run it, accepting the admin prompt and licence.
Pick an install location; on the components screen make sure Git Bash stays ticked.
Accept the defaults on every remaining screen, including the default start-menu folder, and keep pressing Next until it finishes.

concepts.heading: Verifying in VS Code
points: Open Terminal > New Terminal, then use the dropdown beside the + button to choose Git Bash.
A working Git Bash terminal shows a $ prompt.
(Extra) The dropdown is a list of shell profiles; Git Bash only appears once Git for Windows is installed.

concepts.heading: Making Git Bash the default
points: Open View > Command Palette and run Terminal: Select Default Profile, then choose Git Bash.
Close the current terminal and open a new one; the profile label now reads bash.
(Extra) Shortcut for the palette is Ctrl+Shift+P.

task.name: Set up Git Bash in VS Code (Windows)
task.starting_point: Windows machine with VS Code installed.
task.goal: New VS Code terminals open in Git Bash by default.
steps: Download and install Git for Windows with Git Bash selected.
Open a terminal in VS Code and choose Git Bash from the profile dropdown.
Run Select Default Profile from the Command Palette and pick Git Bash.
Open a fresh terminal and confirm it shows bash with a $ prompt.
(Extra) Optionally run git --version in the new terminal; a version number confirms Git for Windows is installed and on the PATH.
task.expected_result: A bash terminal opens by default in VS Code.

pitfalls: Mac users do not need this lesson.
Existing terminals keep their old profile; open a new one after changing the default.

gaps_and_ideas: (Extra) Optional: a short 'Terminal setup check' card at the start of a future command-line lesson, with Windows (Git Bash) and macOS (Terminal/zsh) tabs and a first command to try (pwd), so learners confirm their shell works before the simulator exercises.
